en: In this general introduction to the superficial exposition of this sutra, the Great Master (Zhiyi) composed the *Xuanyan* (Profound Text), and Fazhi further elaborated upon it with his two commentaries (*Ji*). These works open up the profound depths and advance the beginning stages;

their treatment of phenomena and principle is perfectly harmonious and thorough. Truly, they constitute a scripture of ultimate vastness and subtle refinement. How could those of later generations dare to add superfluous words? I shall merely follow this model.

The Master analyzed and distinguished the verses, categorizing them according to their natural spontaneity. The meanings were so detailed and intricate that beginners seeking instruction found it difficult to follow his guidance.
Consequently, during successive lectures, he polished the teachings with simple language; yet to the Patriarch, these appeared as mere skin and hair, or like common pebbles and quartz.
Yet it has been treated like the hair of a castrated horse and cast aside. This student has preserved it in his records, titling it "Superficial Discourse" (Fūsē).

For although the skin and flesh are shallow, they are parts of the human body that one does not discard. Thus, this discourse—though perhaps as slight as a mote of dust or a fine mist—is intended merely to assist the lofty and profound.

How could I dare claim to have seen even a single fragment of its truth? Nor do I intend for it to be considered a novel theory. Whether it be understood by me or censured by me, I shall not decline to accept the consequences.
Thus it is. Written by the Bhikṣu Lingyao of Zhijue Jiaoxi Temple on the first month of the year Wumu (the tenth month).

This chapter concerns the person and the Dharma of the uniquely wondrous Honored One who circulates [this teaching]; therefore, its fundamental purport is roughly identical to that of the main body of the treatise.

Now, the World-Honored One, desiring to fully propagate the wondrous Dharma throughout the world, first universally observed whether the faculties and capacities of those in the world were suitable or not;

he subsequently bestowed his wondrous voice accordingly. Thus, at Vairocana’s Assembly [Huayan], it was presented in brief; at the Deer Park [Śrāvastī], it was revealed in secret; at the Vaipulya [Prajñāpāramitā] stage, it was taught through direct address;

and at the Prajñā [stage], it was explained with explicit clarity. Having now arrived at Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, he may universally open [the teaching] so that the people of the ten worlds may all return to this uniquely wondrous truth.
Furthermore, one observes that the capacities of sentient beings in the world are distinguished as superior, middling, and inferior.

The Buddha, accordingly, employs the sounds of Dharma, parables, and causes and conditions to widely open the gates of expedient means. Thus we know that when the Tathāgata desires to reveal the uniquely wondrous [Dharma], he does not act impulsively;

rather, having carefully observed the capacities of the world, he then extends his guidance. Now, the Great Being who circulates this uniquely wondrous [teaching] is precisely able to reverently embody the sacred model.

First observing the capacities of sentient beings, one then adapts the sound of the Dharma to them. As explained in the separate verses concerning "sound" (*śabda*), the wondrous Dharma is circulated through three cycles by means of three kinds of sounds;

therefore, he is named Avalokiteśvara. "Observing" (*avalokita*) refers to the Great Being’s original Great Radiance Treasury (*mahā-ābhāsaraśmi-garbha*), the perfect illumination of *prajñā*, which silently discerns the capacities of beings through the mind.
"World" (*loka*) refers to the universal manifestation of the body through the body-mystery (*kāya-guhya*), as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*’s [Ten]...
Regarding the marks and embellishments of the body, the treatise discusses two types of "ten bodies": the primary (the Buddha-body) and the secondary (the environment).
These include the land-body and the world-body. As in this sutra, for those who are to be delivered by the Buddha’s world-body, he manifests the Buddha’s world-body;
for those who are to be delivered by the nine world-bodies, he manifests the nine world-bodies. In total, this is because the Great Being [the Bodhisattva] is unimpeded within the Dharma-realm.
The Body-Cloud: This enters the inconceivable, indeterminate, transformative meditation (*nirmāṇa-dhyāna*), wherein the Dharma-body universally manifests before all sentient beings.

The Sound: This is the Great Being’s fourfold unimpeded eloquence (*pratisaṃvid*), which is universally preached for the sake of sentient beings; it is the Dharma that enables those who hear the sound of the teaching to attain liberation.
That is to say, the gate of letters is itself liberation; this is the preaching of the Dharma through the secret of speech (*vāk-guhya*). These are the three virtues and the three [mysteries].
The Esoteric (Mitsu) is the Middle Way that has been long cultivated and long realized by the Great Being (Bodhisattva), corresponding to the fundamental source.

Although it is achieved through the cultivation of the three contemplations (*san-gen*), if one were to utter it as a single phrase, it could be pointed to as the Perfect Middle (*en-chū*) corresponding to the fundamental source.

Having attained this Middle Way corresponding to the fundamental source, one may then, within the gateway of conventional truth (*zokutai-mon*), employ the wondrous provisional (*myō-ke*) to universally transform sentient beings. Yet, in the process of transforming sentient beings, one does not depart from compassion (*ji*).

"Compassion and Deliverance. If one reads "Guānzì" (Contemplating the Word) as one phrase and "Shìyīn" (World-Sound) as another, this represents the Great Being who is eternally illuminating while remaining in stillness.

Universally reflecting the sounds of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, bells, chimes, gongs, drums, men, women, those of the Two Vehicles, Bodhisattvas, and the ten worlds who call upon him in distress, he causes them all to attain liberation. This is the Great Being amidst dispersion...
This is the vow made by the Buddha Ratnagarbha of the Trailokya realm:

"If any sentient beings in the world who call upon my name do not escape suffering, I vow not to attain perfect enlightenment. In the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, it is stated that one should all recite my name with a sincere mind;
now, as soon as they hear my voice in this sutra, they shall all attain liberation. [In the] *Śūraṅgama-samādhi-sūtra* (Lengyan), the lower section concerns the Dharma...
"Sentient beings in the realms share the same sorrowful longing" refers to the compassionate contemplation that uproots suffering.

If the two characters "guānshì" (觀世) are read as a single phrase and "yīzì" (一字) is read as a separate phrase, then it means that the Great Being universally contemplates the differences in the capacities and conditions of the ten worlds.
Thereafter, one adapts the Dharma according to the occasion. This is as described in the present sutra:

for those who are to be delivered by manifesting a body within a particular world, one manifests a body within that very world and preaches the Dharma so that they may attain liberation; this is preceded by first discerning their capacities through the secret of mind (*mantra-guhyaka*).
Subsequently, he preached the Dharma by means of the wheel of speech. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Above, he shares the same power of compassion as the Buddhas of the ten directions.

This refers to the contemplation of compassion that bestows happiness. In essence, the provisional contemplations used to deliver sentient beings and the transformations established according to conventional truth do not go beyond the acts of bestowing compassion and pulling [beings] out of suffering.
Nevertheless, in the world, people often refer only to "Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva" or "Avalokiteśvara Mahāsattva," omitting the middle character.
The single character "Jian" (間) is also sufficient to exhaustively encompass the virtues of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

For this character "Guan" (觀) is precisely the Great Being’s initial cultivation of the threefold contemplation within a single mind; and the single character "Yin" (音) is the single realm of the three truths.

This is what is meant by the "eternal realm being signless" and "eternal wisdom being non-conditioned. One understands this through names and words, cultivates this through contemplative practice, until finally the beginning and the fundamental merge as one.

When both the beginning and the root are forgotten, then the three truths, the three contemplations, and the three negations of the three are realized: to raise one is to have all three, and the three are identical to the one.
Since the names of truth and contemplation differ while their substance is the same, the duality of subject and object is non-dual.

As stated in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, when [the Buddha] first received instruction from the Tathāgata Guanyin (Avalokiteśvara), he entered samādhi through hearing, reflection, and cultivation; he first entered it within the realm of hearing.

The flow of thought forgets its source. Once that which is entered has become still, the two characteristics of motion and stillness clearly cease to arise. Thus, hearing is exhausted and that which is heard is also exhausted;
the awareness of what is perceived is empty, and this emptiness-awareness reaches ultimate perfection. With the cessation of arising and ceasing, quiescent extinction manifests before one.
Suddenly transcending both the mundane and supramundane worlds, one takes the very sounds previously heard as the object and contemplates them with perfect observation.

This is the contemplation that directly shatters the ten realms and the five stages of abiding to reveal the true emptiness and wash away all marks. Question: The contemplation of emptiness (kōngguān) only breaks the four abidings and the six classes of ordinary beings.
Now you say that "quiescent extinction manifests before one," which implies that both the provisional and the real are inherently within emptiness.

How can you say it is merely the contemplation of emptiness washing away marks? Answer: In the sequential three contemplations of the Separate Teaching (Biéjiā), the contemplation of emptiness through which the Tripitaka and Shared Teachings enter the Way only...

This breaks through the four abidings and the six mundane realms. What the Great Being now cultivates is the perfect and wondrous contemplation of the Truths: when empty, the ten realms are all empty;
when established, the ten realms are all established. This is identical to the Three Truths; it is also called the Truth of Reality (*tattva-satya*), which dissolves all phenomena.
How could it be merely a partial truth or a small emptiness? Therefore, this perfect emptiness stands before us; it not only destroys the four abidings but also destroys ignorance (*avidyā*).
It not only destroys the six classes of ordinary beings but also destroys the ten realms. Only then can it be called "suddenly transcending the mundane and supramundane worlds.
This is just as when the three characters of Avalokiteśvara were first explained: they are themselves the Middle Way, Reality, and the Response.
How could it be that this is merely a matter of sequential progression?
It is truly because the Great Being possesses such perfect and wondrous sublime virtue that he is bestowed with the elegant name "Avalokiteśvara" (The One Who Observes the Sounds of the World).

One who has perfected such wondrous contemplation produces such perfect and wondrous sounds; thus, he is able to circulate the Tathāgata’s subtle Dharma. How could anyone else possibly be compared to him? ○
Regarding the Bodhisattva: since a Great Being (Mahāsattva) who possesses perfect virtue is equal to a Buddha, how much more so when he was already the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa in the past?
He should not still occupy the rank of a Bodhisattva.

A Bodhisattva is the rank of the junior disciple among teacher and disciple, the rank of the minister among ruler and subject, and the rank of the son among father and son. This has two meanings. First:

This is the modesty of this Great Being. Indeed, the Original Teacher is also named Avalokiteśvara; it is precisely because he has successfully inherited the legacy of his predecessor—just as when the square ladle is full, the water is full—that he is also named Avalokiteśvara.
However, just as a son does not dare call his father "old" while the father is still living, he humbly occupies the position of the son.
Furthermore, as he currently resides within the precious pond in the World of Ultimate Bliss (Sukhāvatī) as the successor, he properly occupies the rank of a son.
Regarding his rank: although he has now come to this Sahā world as a guest, since he has come to assist in the transformation of beings, he stands as an equal among the disciples.
It should not be otherwise. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "I vow to occupy the rank of a Dharma Prince beneath the various Buddhas of the ten directions.
This reflects the Bodhisattva’s habitual humility and modesty; he dwells in a state of self-effacement, unlike the arrogance and conceit of worldly people. Second is...
The compassion of a Great Being (Mahāsattva) is such that, because he occupies the station of a Buddha, he is so exalted and sublime that it is difficult for him to rescue and deliver others.

It is like a Son of Heaven dwelling deep within the nine-layered palace: although he may issue great favors and a general amnesty, wishing to extend them universally to all living beings, how can he do so when the Emperor’s pardon does not reach the officials, and the officials’ pardon does not reach the subordinates?
Furthermore, if there is a grant from the treasury, it remains with the high-ranking officials...
It is concealed; it is stolen away by lowly servants. Thus, the common people are unable to personally bask in the sublime virtue of their superiors.
Therefore, among the great men of antiquity, there were those who harbored a grievance for never having served as a district magistrate.

Although the Great Being’s own person was already that of a Buddha, he seemed to slight the position of the Son of Heaven and refused to assume it, instead choosing to dwell contentedly in the rank of a Bodhisattva in order to universally uproot the suffering of sentient beings and universally bestow [upon them]...

The joy of sentient beings is like the Great Compassion of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*. What is spoken of in this present sutra is that which can manifest both the real and the provisional, can ascend and descend, can advance and retreat, and can bend and believe;
it is like a gentleman who is not limited to a single vessel, being suitable for any role on either side.

Furthermore, it shares with Śākyamuni the great power of sovereign mastery (*mahopāya-vaśitā*) and the wondrous capability of being able to act in any way whatsoever, unlike the dragon at the peak of its strength.
To be without a head, able to ascend but unable to descend, and able to advance but unable to retreat—such is the constrained practice of the lesser sages.
○ In the "Universal Gate" chapter, the various Bodhisattvas, in their self-cultivation and transformation of others, each abide in a single Dharma-gate;
for example, Mañjuśrī takes wisdom as his gate, while Samantabhadra takes practice as his gate. Now, the reason this Great Being’s gate is named "Universal" (Pumen) is precisely...
This is identical to the wondrous Dharma taught by the Founder. For the Dharma-gate realized and bestowed by the Founder is difficult to understand and difficult to enter;
it is called "wondrous" because it is neither sudden nor gradual, neither secret nor indeterminate, and does not belong to the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, or Complete teachings.
It is not through the four gates of the Āgamas that one enters the Cool Pond together with the three types of practitioners by means of wordlessness.
Within the Vermilion Bird Gate of the Azure Dragon Palace—the gateway where the substance of the Way enters emptiness—there is no hindrance to the coming and going of the common people.
This is not the gate of the fifty-three spiritual friends of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, nor the forty-two letter-gates, nor the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of dhāraṇīs, samādhis, and pāramitās;
yet when sentient beings respond with sincere invocation, the Tathāgata does not hinder the bestowing [of his grace].
Whether it be sudden giving, gradual giving, secret giving, or indeterminate giving; whether it be the Treasuries, the Shared, the Distinct, or the Perfect;

even unto the eighty-four thousand dharanis, samadhis, and paramitas—these dharmas are not obstructed by being simultaneously sudden, gradual, secret, indeterminate, or belonging to the Treasuries, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect, even unto the eighty-four thousand paramita dharmas. Therefore...
It is called "wondrous. As for why the Dharma practiced and bestowed by the Great Being for the purpose of uprooting suffering and bringing joy is called "universal" (pu):

it is because this gateway is neither great nor small, neither square nor round, neither sudden nor gradual, nor secret nor indeterminate, and so on, up to being none of the eighty-four thousand dharanis, samadhis, or paramitas, yet it is able to accord with...

When the resonance of the capacity for awakening strikes, it does not hinder the opening of the various teachings—Great, Small, Square, Round, Sudden, Gradual, Esoteric, Indeterminate, Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Complete—nor even the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates of samādhi and dhāraṇī.

These are used to universally uproot the suffering of the dharma-realm, to universally bestow the bliss of the dharma-realm, and to universally respond to the seekers among sentient beings. One should know that if one dwells fixedly in a single dharma, [one cannot fulfill these functions].

A single gate cannot universally accommodate all capacities or respond to everyone. Although one does not dwell in attachment to a single gate, it is also not the case that there is no fundamental basis to rely upon.

Therefore, it does not hinder the fact that the Great and Small Vehicles, the square and round, the Sudden and Gradual, the Secret and Indeterminate, and the Tripitaka, Shared, Distinct, and Perfect teachings are identical;
that is, they all enter through the four gates. Just as the Vermilion Bird Gate does not obstruct the entry and exit of commoners, this extends even to the eight [directions].
This is the Dharma-gate of the Perfection of Samādhi through fourteen thousand dhāraṇīs; therefore, it is called "Universal" (Pǔ).

The World-Honored One Śākyamuni realized this upon the nature and characteristics of the three-thousandfold world system by means of the perfect three contemplations (*yuán sānguān*), whereby all are the true reality (*shíxiàng*).

Thus, he was able to exercise mastery over both contraction and expansion. Likewise, the Great Being [the Bodhisattva] also realized all immeasurable Dharma-gates by means of the perfect three contemplations.
This is the true reality (*dharmatā*). Therefore, it is able to provide salvation and deliverance without restriction. Thus we know that the Dharma is the gate, and the gate is the Dharma;
the universal is the wondrous, and the wondrous is the universal. They are non-dual and without distinction.

Such a wondrous Dharma cannot be circulated except through the Universal Gate; only such a Universal Gate can circulate this wondrous Dharma. This is not the same as [the teachings] of other bodhisattvas.
Each resides in a single gate and does not necessarily encompass all aspects.

Therefore, it is said that the person and dharma of the "Excellence of Sole Propagation" are roughly identical in their essential purport to the True School (Zhengzong). As for the ten pairs and five singles, they are fully detailed in the *Xuanyi* (Profound Record).

This is the prose section from the "Zhengshuo" (Correct Exposition) of the *Shuowen*. The Great Master [Xuanzang] interpreted the sutra through three explanations and established the structural divisions and definitions.

Not only does it surpass the *Lüshi Chunqiu*, where not even a single character could be altered for a thousand pieces of gold; now, following the Grand Master’s broad outline, I have composed two chapters. The first...

This [section] on Avalokiteśvara’s rescue from suffering is followed by that on the Universal Gate’s bestowal of happiness. The former concludes with the exhortation to uphold the name after the extraction of suffering;

the latter concludes with the exhortation to make offerings after the universal manifestation. Although each section contains the three karmas of both bestowing and extracting, for the sake of the general meaning, they are broadly divided as follows;
even in the subsequent verse section, there are only these two chapters on bestowing and extracting, which are explained in the independent verses.

The two characters "Guanyin" (Avalokiteśvara) are also explained by interpreting "guan" (contemplation) as the extraction of suffering and "yin" (sound) as the bestowal of bliss. This concludes the individual verses;

only then does the general eulogy provide the two meanings of exhorting one to uphold [the name] and exhorting one to make offerings. Indeed, these two—extracting [suffering] and bestowing [bliss]—are sufficient to exhaustively encompass the compassion of the Great Being;

there is no need for further separate explanations. It has been inferred that when the Great Being departed from the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī) to come to this Sahā world, his primary intention was to guide and receive sentient beings.

It is his original intention that he may bring all sentient beings who dwell in this world of endurance (*saha*) to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*Sukhāvatī*), manifesting immeasurable bodies to preach the Dharma and bestow upon them the bliss of transcendence.

However, since the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) here entail heavy transgressions and much suffering, it is appropriate first to extract them from their pain—just as when a disease is urgent, one must first treat its external symptoms.
This is especially true for those in this land who are inferior and thus called "enduring"; unless there were a great calamity, [he would not have acted otherwise].

What great suffering! To be so addicted to the coarse and debased five desires as to take them for pleasure, unable to turn the mind toward the Way—until calamities such as water, fire, blades, and bandits arrive at one's head, and there is nothing that can be done, only then does one think of seeking the aid of the Great Being (Mahāsattva).

If the Great Being, because of one’s habitual indolence and the fact that one seeks help only when in extreme suffering, were not to rescue and deliver one, then this person would be truly obstinate and deluded.

Sentient beings would never have the opportunity to resolve their minds toward liberation from suffering; furthermore, this is not the Universal Gate through which Great Beings deliver others from suffering.

Therefore, when a Great Being hears even a single invocation during a time of urgent distress, they become the object of that Great Being’s compassionate mind, immediately causing the being to be freed from suffering.
It is like water in a basin and the moon in the sky meeting in a convergence of response and stimulus, forming the causal conditions for the awakening of the practitioner. From this...
Once they have been liberated from suffering, they are then able to turn their hearts with sincere devotion toward [the Dharma], and I can gradually bestow upon them the joy of the Dharma.

Thus, does the Great Being not desire to immediately grant the happiness of all sentient beings in the world? It is simply that the circumstances are not yet possible. Even within this process of extracting them from suffering...
Furthermore, one must first attend to what is most urgent. For instance, when entering water or fire, the retribution for one's obstacles has already arrived;

whether measured by kalpas or by mere moments, life is but a fleeting instant, and there is no possibility of escape. Yet, at the final moment, one calls out to the Great Being like an ignorant child;
having already fallen into water or fire, with no one known to them in their heart and no method to free themselves from suffering, they can do nothing but wail and cry out.
Regarding parents: one should immediately crawl upon one's belly to rescue them, without the slightest delay. Therefore, the seven calamities are dealt with first.

As for the three poisons within the mind, although they are sufficient to harm the body and invite retribution—requiring one to undergo both present and future suffering—the matter is somewhat more gradual;
thus, they follow next. Whether it be lack of sons or daughters, though these are called evil retributions, they are still matters external to the person.

Having specifically dwelt among them after their suffering was removed, you, Great Being, have again come to our Sahā world with the intention of transforming my sentient beings so that they may sever the bonds of craving and emerge from birth and death.
Yet now, this person seeks a son or a daughter; this is entirely the sticky glue of greed and attachment, a matter of lingering within birth and death.
Why, Great Being, do you instead fulfill such a request? Thus, the Mother has lost her original purpose for coming from the East.

Is this so? It is most certainly not. This is a world of rigidity and strength where sentient beings are ignorant and deluded; evil thoughts arise easily, while a virtuous mind is difficult to produce.
The Great Being sought in many ways for even a single spark of inclination toward the good in him, but could find none at all.

Now, because having no descendants would constitute the ultimate unfiliality, and since he would not relinquish his wealth and property, it would pass to others upon his death. Therefore, [he wished to...]

They were seeking male or female offspring. On ordinary days, they had never offered worship or made offerings to the Mahāsattva; it was only because of their private petition that they temporarily paid him respect.

If the Mahāsattva were to despise their folly and fail to grant their request, then the foolish people’s malice would only increase further, and they would forever sever their connection with the Mahāsattva.
Therefore, by granting their improper request, he leads them out toward the Buddha.
With such a mind, one can gradually guide others through skillful means, leading them step by step to transcend suffering and attain joy, thereby enabling them to escape birth and death.
This so-called method of first using the hook of desire to entice them and later leading them into the Buddha-way is something that these bodhisattvas would find beneath their dignity to perform.
Yet it is Avalokiteśvara alone who is able to condescend to such [beings].

Moreover, since the Great Being has long realized the Samādhi of the Mother of Wisdom and constantly serves as a Dharma Prince to the Buddhas of the ten directions, this is simply what is appropriately arranged within his Universal Gate (Pumen).
This is what is called "that which arises from the accumulation of righteousness"; it is not a mere accidental hit achieved without a foundation. Furthermore, the Great Being—
The gate that is opened is named "Universal" (Pumen). It is just like the armory of a king’s general, wherein there is not a single dharma that is not contained.
If worldly people seek sons or daughters and these are not granted, then the name and reality of the Universal Gate would be lost.

This is truly because worldly people seek the six perfections and myriad practices, the five cessations and four foundations of mindfulness, the meditative concentrations of phenomena and principle, and the mundane wholesome virtues. Indeed...
He gives to all without exception. Thus, by means of the entanglements sought through the heart of ignorant attachment, he is like a great bell suspended on its stand:
when struck, it rings; when a thousand conditions arise simultaneously, [the responses] surge like clouds and fall like springs. Even cow urine and horse dung are kept by the physician;
only then can he be called one of the Universal Gate (Samantamukha).
In the section on the exhortation to uphold the Name, there are three parts: first, a general summary of the three karmas to indicate the practice of upholding the Name;

second, a comparative analysis of the partial and the perfect to manifest its merit; and third, the conclusion showing that the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara, as received by Akṣayamati, bestows such immeasurable and boundless benefits of merit and virtue.
Regarding the first part, the general summary indicating the practice, it says: "If..."
If there are sentient beings who respectfully revere and pay homage to Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, their merit shall not be in vain.
For this reason, all sentient beings should uphold the name of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. This is for three reasons.

First, because by upholding the name as described above—reverently mindful and paying homage—one will certainly attain liberation from suffering, have poisons removed, and fulfill one's aspirations; therefore it is said: "If there are sentient beings who... [and so forth].
"Reverently prostrating, merit shall not be in vain. This single phrase concludes the various meanings previously discussed.

Therefore, "one should all receive and uphold the Name"—this single phrase is an exhortation to uphold it. One should know that while the previous statement, "reverently prostrate," necessarily implies the inclusion of upholding the Name, the subsequent statement, "one should all receive and uphold the Name," necessarily encompasses reverent prostration. Thus, the conclusion and the exhortation are expressed through mutual implication.
Thus, it can be understood that they are mutually complete. For since the preceding [passage] already mentioned the two karmas of body and mind, how could the karma of speech not be included?
And since the subsequent [passage] speaks only of "holding the name," how could the other two karmas not be included? This is the skillful means of the Honored One’s teaching;

therefore, by presenting each from one side, the meaning of their mutual completion is made manifest. This is truly because the three karmas have been invoked as described above, and thus merit is never in vain.

If one does not abandon [this practice], one will immediately attain the wondrous response of the three karmas. For this reason, all sentient beings should respectfully prostrate and receive and uphold the Name;
it is not in vain. This is as stated in the subsequent separate verse: "Hearing the Name, seeing the body and mind, and mindfulness—these three words do not pass by in vain.
Second, the text states: "If one says that prostrating fulfills one's vows, there are indeed those who prostrate yet do not receive [the fulfillment]."
If one’s wishes are fulfilled, how can it be said that [the practice] is not in vain? The commentary states: Because the mind lacks resolve, the wish remains unfulfilled;
yet the merit of prostration provides hidden support that is never lost. This is like the repentance in the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*:

although one does not see light or flowers, one still gains the increase of receiving the precepts. Therefore, one should perform prostrations and uphold [the practice]. Third, the question: Now, by means of...

There are those who invoke the name in times of distress; there are those who harbor poisonous thoughts; there are those who seek [blessings] through prostration. Only after these acts can one be liberated from suffering.
If there were people in the world who experienced neither distress nor harbored poisonous thoughts, nor had any requests, then it would seem that prostration and invocation were unnecessary;

prostration and invocation would likewise be useless and devoid of merit. Answer: Even if one is without distress or requests, if there is prostration and reverence, the merit will not be in vain. As for those with requests...
Thus, it is certainly not in vain to discard [the practice]. Even without seeking ritual observance, one obtains even greater merit; therefore, it is not wasted.

This is truly because when there are difficulties, merely reciting the name can bring liberation from suffering; thus, one must certainly maintain ritual observance. When there are no difficulties, merely reciting the name ensures that the merit is not wasted.
Therefore, all should receive and uphold [the Buddha’s] name; if there is poison, it will be immediately removed. One should certainly pay respect;

even if one has no specific need for protection, by paying respect, merit will not be in vain. For this reason, all should receive and uphold [the name]. If there is a request, it will surely be fulfilled; one must certainly perform prostrations.

Even if one has no request, by performing prostrations, merit will not be in vain. Therefore, one should perform prostrations, mindfulness, and the recitation of the name. Thus we know that for those who have requests...

One should certainly pay homage and recite [the name]. Those who are free from seeking should especially pay homage and recite it. The single word "all" (皆) universally points to all sentient beings in the world.
For those who pay homage and recite because they have a request or face a difficulty, such people are not many.

Now, since even those who have no requests and no difficulties can recite and pay homage without it being in vain, then everyone in the world ought to pay homage, recite, and uphold the Name. Therefore—

[The Master] said: "All [the three modes of practice] are appropriate. Question: Since you have generally concluded by exhorting the maintenance of the three karmas through prostration, why is it that when we reach the section below, you only compare the merit based on the maintenance of the Name?
Answer: If even the minor goodness of maintaining the Name with a single vocal karma yields inexhaustible merit, how much more so is the merit of inwardly reverently and constantly recollecting it?
And how much more so is the merit of prostrating and making offerings?
How virtuous! When there are hardships or petitions, even the merit of maintaining the ritual is already inexhaustible;
how much more so the merit cultivated during the ordinary course of daily life when there are neither hardships nor petitions? This is the subtle skill with which the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma:

by comparing the minor merit of merely upholding the name, it is sufficient to illustrate the profound efficacy of mindfulness and ritual, as well as the constancy of cultivation even in the absence of petitioning.
His virtue is immeasurable and boundless.
Within the "Universal Gateway Manifestations," as for why only several celestial kings appear in the heavenly realm while both the great and the small appear in the human realm:

it is because the male and female deities and other celestial subjects are all ordinary beings who have practiced [the path] and departed [from the world]; yet, their attachment to pleasure is already deep.
Reflecting on impermanence: although the Great Being manifested entry among those classes of beings, they did not turn their minds [toward awakening];

how much less so for the celestial subjects, who take the pleasures of their own realm as ultimate and lack any separate aspiration for the Buddha-dharma. It seems as though there were no one who shared his intent.
Therefore, the Great Being manifests entry among those classes, acting as their ruler or sovereign; yet transcending them all, he cultivates and realizes the Buddha-dharma.
By his own majestic power, he universally transforms his subjects and citizens, such that they naturally emulate his superior conduct and gradually draw their hearts toward him.

This is like the descriptions in the *Avalokiteśvara-ādhyeṣaṇā-sūtra*, where Avalokiteśvara appears as a celestial being, a hero, or the Great Brahmā of profound distance. All these manifestations appear.
Acting as a sovereign to counteract the self-importance of ministers and subjects:

the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that among those in the five Pure Abodes of the fourth dhyāna, as well as their celestial kings, there is only the reverent hearing of his name but no direct vision of him.
This is because they are all great empowered Bodhisattvas manifesting within those realms. Examining this manifestation here is sufficient to dispel doubts regarding that scripture.
It is the mind. That the male and female, the noble and the humble, all appear within the human realm is precisely because one can regulate the mental faculties and direct them toward Bodhi;

this is possible only through the human path. Furthermore, as suffering and joy alternate in the human world, there are those who record the *Prajñāpāramitā* to admonish themselves regarding impermanence.
Although the resolve to awaken may not yet be fixed, the karmic capacities of all ten realms are fully present within the human realm. Humans are capable of realization; humans are [the vessel].
It is clearly seen that since the Great Being has come to the human realm to preach the Dharma, he frequently manifests in human form.

However, these thirty-two manifestations are merely a brief enumeration of the beginning; as for the Great Being’s universal gate of manifestation, it is like the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* describing the appearance of a thousand hands and eyes, or the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* describing eighty-four thousand bodies and hands—truly beyond measure. For instance, when manifesting as a golden infant...
The wife [of the Buddha], the wife of the horse-herder, Empress Wencheng of the Tang as a clam, Emperor Daizong of the Tang within an egg,
and the transformation of Feng Juqu into the tusk of a pig— how could these few instances possibly exhaust the sovereign freedom of the Universal Gate?

Following the section on the Universal Gate bestowing joy, the exhortation to provide offerings concludes by stating that even those who offer great worship have never failed to employ the three karmas [of body, speech, and mind].

If one ought to courageously undertake such a great matter as major offering, how much more so should one apply oneself with diligence to the secondary practices of mental recollection and verbal invocation?
Previously, the shallow nature of holding the name was contrasted with the profound depth of bodily and mental practice; now, [the text continues...]
Thus, the magnitude of this offering is such that it surpasses even the second level of devotion involving both mind and speech; no skill in preaching the Dharma exceeds this.

One should understand that in the previous section on the holding of the name, sixty-two billion Bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges were compared with a single Avalokiteśvara, and the merit of these two was shown to be exactly equal and without distinction. Now, why is no such comparison presented within this section on offerings?

This is but one aspect of the measure. One must know that even the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati, who dwells upon the earth, still seeks the compassionate protection of Avalokiteśvara by offering him the *dharmaparyāya-maṇiratna-avalambana* (the jeweled necklace of the dharma-gate) cultivated through kalpas of practice.

Thus, one can understand that the merit of making offerings to other bodhisattvas and the merit of making offerings to the Great Being Avalokiteśvara are not merely as different as heaven and earth, but are inconceivable by any factor of ten, hundred, or more. Furthermore...

Furthermore, these necklaces were offered as a superior gift; they were merely material offerings (*āmiṣadāna*). Why, then, does Akṣayamati say that he has received this precious necklace as a gift of Dharma (*dharmadāna*)?

It is because Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages have practiced through successive kalpas and have already entered the stage of true retribution (*vipākabhūmi*), where both merit and wisdom flourish.
Thus, they all adorn their bodies with the jewels of the Dharma-gates, as the *Avataṃsaka* Sūtra describes the precious regalia of Vairocana.

Regarding the practice [of offering necklaces]: the *Lotus Sūtra* speaks of the "necklace-wearing elder" (*mālā-dhara-gṛhapati*). Is this not precisely because his body—the Dharma-gate—is adorned with the jewels of merit?
Just as a worldly pauper who has failed to cultivate merit from of old dies of cold and hunger, his body uncovered by clothing;
so too is the case for one who plants roots of merit, who possesses garments of pearls and food of jade. Thus, the offering of the necklace is precisely that which...
The practice of this dharma-gate is an act of giving. Within this context, Avalokiteśvara did not accept it.
Wujinyi (Akṣayamati) ascended once more and, employing the Honored One as an intermediary to smooth the way, he offered it so that both parties might attain what is correct.

The Buddha said, "You should have compassion for Akṣayamati, the fourfold assembly, and the eight classes of beings who receive these necklaces. He stated that Akṣayamati’s relinquishment of his offerings was not for the sake of seeking personal merit, but was intended to lead others...
The fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings emulate this by making offerings, thereby forming karmic connections with the Great Being and seeking his deliverance;
this is the earnest resolve of Akṣayamati. O Avalokiteśvara, you should take pity on his heart for the sake of the multitude and accept these necklaces;
thus it is said, "you should take pity on Akṣayamati. How much more so now that Akṣayamati has taken the lead in making this offering!
He leads the rest of the assembly. If the Great Being does not accept [the offerings], then the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings witness this refusal;
they all find excuses, saying, "The Great Being will not accept," and thus are unwilling to give or to form a karmic connection with the Great Being.

Would this not forever sever the wholesome conditions for sentient beings? Now, I exhort Avalokiteśvara to graciously accept the offerings, thereby opening the gateway for sentient beings to practice making offerings.
All shall follow the superior example and emulate those below, thereby forming a karmic affinity with the Sage; thus, there will come a time of liberation from birth and death. Therefore it is said:

"Compassionately bestow this necklace upon the fourfold assembly and the eight classes of beings. This exhortation is sufficient to show that the giver acts for others and not for self, clearly manifesting a heart of compassion.
The recipient likewise acts for others and not for material things; the giving and receiving are both practical and appropriate. Since these words have been spoken...

The Middle Way is correct in its reception; thus, Avalokiteśvara accepted it immediately. Now, as for the Mahāsattvas of the Dharma-body, they certainly act for the sake of the Dharma and for the sake of sentient beings during the process of receiving [offerings].
Yet, the wicked people of this Sahā world are extremely difficult to reach through conversion.
They would then watch from the sidelines with cold indifference, claiming that they saw the encounter with the Sage and saying, "Avalokiteśvara has come like a merchant or a peddler to deceive me."

The *Ābharaṇa* (Necklace) of the Eastern Land has departed. Guanyin manifested this to shield people of evil intent and wrong views from falling into greedy attachment, and thus he immediately returned it to be offered to the two sages.

Wujinyi, as for your question regarding how one can roam the Sahā world to preach the Dharma for sentient beings—this is sufficient to demonstrate the Great Being’s sovereign spiritual power to roam the Sahā world and transform those of evil nature.
△ Second, the "Separate Verses" (Bieji). Originally, this was the *Universal Gateway* (Pumen) section in verse form; it is now termed "Separate Verses" for two reasons:
first, these were not translated by Master Kumārajīva at the same time as the prose, but were translated separately by Jñānagupta during the Sui dynasty;

second, they do not merely repeat the prose in verse, but also include additional verses, the *Extraction of Vows and Practices* (Baxingyuan), and a separate commentary on the two characters of "Avalokiteśvara."

Furthermore, because it differs slightly from the prose (*gadya*) in its appearance and disappearance, the Vinaya Master says that the remaining verses of the individual chapters (*varga*) refer to this very section.
It is divided into three parts: first, the restatement of the sūtra text; second, the specific explanation of Avalokiteśvara; and third, the concluding summary of the recitation and offerings.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the question.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Akṣayamati asked in verse: "World-Honored One, endowed with wondrous marks, I now ask you again:
For what causes and conditions is this Son of the Buddha named Avalokiteśvara?"

△ Second, the section on the answer, which is divided into two parts. First, the dual introduction; second, the actual presentation of giving and uprooting. First, Avalokiteśvara’s uprooting of suffering:
“The Honored One endowed with wondrous marks replied in verse to Akṣayamati: ‘Listen to the practice of Avalokiteśvara.’”
While each of the bodhisattvas has their own specific gate of practice, Avalokiteśvara alone takes the extraction of suffering through great compassion as his primary activity.

As seen in the sixteen vows of the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra*, the first four great vows prioritize the liberation of sentient beings from suffering, while the latter six vows specifically counteract the sufferings of the four realms of existence.
Furthermore, this is also evident in the six [vows] within the *Sutra on the Invocation of Avalokiteśvara*.
Avalokiteśvara confronts and breaks through the six realms of existence. His great compassion and great kindness, like the fearless lion, cause his great light to shine universally;

this is primarily based on the principle of remedial treatment (*pratipakṣa*). It correctly returns to the extraction of suffering. Therefore, this phrase indicates that the aforementioned Avalokiteśvara extracts [beings] from suffering.
△ Second, the Universal Gate bestows happiness.
It skillfully responds to all directions and locations;
it may be known by its various manifested forms as it wanders through all lands.

△ Second, the extended verses on practice and vows. "Extended" means supplementary. While the sutra text clarifies only bestowing and extracting, it does not reveal the root of bestowing and extracting;
these are now supplemented and brought forth, hence they are called "extended."
My great vows are as deep as the ocean; throughout inconceivable kalpas, I have served many thousands of billions of Buddhas and made these vast, pure aspirations.
My vows are like those of the sixteen vows and the twelve vows, and even at the time of the Buddha Ratnagarbha, I vowed:
"If there be any sentient beings who call upon my name and do not attain liberation, I shall not achieve perfect enlightenment. If there be any who recite and uphold [this...]
"Regarding the Great Compassion Dhāraṇī: 'If I do not attain birth in the lands of all Buddhas, I vow not to achieve perfect enlightenment,' and so forth—serving the Buddha is itself practice.
It is like first encountering the Tathāgata Ancient Avalokiteśvara;

after generating the resolve for awakening and attaining fruition, one seeks the Buddha-way above with shared kindness and shared compassion, and transforms sentient beings below. This is like encountering the Tathāgata King of Thousand Rays Abiding in Tranquility."

This refers to such things as "suddenly transcending the eight stages" and so forth. It is because there has long been the foundation of such practices and vows that one is able to manifest infinite bodies and provide salvation without limit.
What was previously called "the practice of Avalokiteśvara" refers to the removal of suffering after attaining the fruit;
what is now "serving the Buddha" refers to that which is cultivated during the causal stage.

△ Second, the dual explanation of the two [sections]. First, the explanation of Avalokiteśvara’s extraction from suffering has three parts. First, a general verse on the cessation of suffering through the three karmas: "I shall briefly explain for you:
hearing my name, seeing my body, or recollecting me in the mind—these do not pass in vain; they can extinguish all sufferings of existence."

In the prose section, [the text] calls out names to extract one from suffering, rescues from the seven calamities, contemplates in the mind to extinguish the three poisons, and through physical prostration fulfills two aspirations.
Now, first, it summarizes these in verse: "Hearing the name, seeing the body, and contemplating in the mind can extinguish all sufferings of existence;

one is immediately freed from the sufferings of the seven calamities and so forth. These seven calamities and two aspirations are explained in terms of the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*), yet fundamentally they pervade the ten realms (*daśadhātu*).

Therefore, it is said "all existences" (*sarvabhava*). By invoking the twenty-five sovereign samādhis of Avalokiteśvara, one universally eradicates the three obstacles of the twenty-five existences until reaching the ultimate limit;
hence, it is said "able to extinguish. In his prose commentary, the Great Master provided three interpretations based on the underlying meaning;
now, within these verses, that very meaning is clearly set forth. One deeply perceives therein the Great Master’s contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
The Buddha— knowing that this is a minor Śākyamuni from the eastern land of the Tathāgata’s secret treasury— uses the three characters “not in vain” (bù kōng guò),
which correspond to the phrase above regarding blessings not being wasted. Having thus provided a general verse on uprooting suffering through the three types of action,
he then extensively expounds upon one specific aspect.

△ Second, the detailed verse on praising the name for rescuing from calamities. It is called "detailed" because while the prose version merely lists seven calamities, the present verse enumerates twelve; hence it is termed "detailed."
Even if one should harbor harmful intent and push another into a great pit of fire, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, that fiery pit shall turn into a pond.
(1) Or if one is adrift upon the vast ocean, facing the perils of fish, dragons, and various ghosts, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, the surging waves shall not drown them.
(2) Or if one stands upon the peak of Mount Sumeru and is pushed over by others, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they will be like the sun in the sky. (3)
(3) Or dwelling in the void, one may be pursued by wicked men and fall upon the Diamond Mountains;
yet by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, not even a single hair can be harmed. (4) Or encountering hostile bandits surrounding one, each wielding a blade to inflict harm;

yet by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they all immediately give rise to a mind of compassion. (5) Or meeting with the suffering of royal punishment, facing execution as life draws to its end; yet by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara...

If one is cut into pieces by a sword (6), or imprisoned and bound with shackles and manacles, with hands and feet in fetters—by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, one shall be released and attain liberation (7).
If there are curses and various poisonous drugs intended to harm the body—by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall return to the person who sent them (8).
Or if one encounters evil rākṣasas, venomous dragons, or various ghosts—by recollecting him...

By the power of Avalokiteśvara, at that time none dare to harm them (9). If they are surrounded by fierce beasts with terrifying sharp fangs and claws, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, they flee swiftly in every direction (10).
Regarding vipers, snakes, and scorpions, whose poisonous breath blazes like smoke and fire—

By recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, they shall turn back upon hearing his voice (11). When clouds and thunder roll, lightning flashes, and hail falls with torrential rain, by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, it shall be dispersed at that very moment (12).
Although the difficulties are twelve, they do not essentially go beyond the six elements of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and consciousness;
they merely present several aspects to manifest the wondrous capabilities of the Great Being. The meaning of the text is thus clear.
△ Third, the summary of the immeasurable salvation from suffering:
When sentient beings are beset by calamities and immeasurable sufferings press upon their bodies, the wondrous power of Avalokiteśvara’s wisdom can rescue them from the sufferings of the world.
In the prose section, it first clarifies the general relief from all sufferings, stating:

"If there are immeasurable hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings undergoing various afflictions and distresses, upon hearing this Bodhisattva’s name and single-mindedly reciting it, Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva immediately perceives their voices and they all attain liberation.
Only after this does it separately set forth the deliverance from the seven calamities. Now...

Having clearly explained the extraction from all calamities, he then summarizes the universal salvation; this is the essence of the mutual clarification between the preceding and succeeding parts of the teaching.
Previously it was said, "hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of sentient beings," and now it is said, "sentient beings in the world.
Previously it was said, "suffering various afflictions," and now it is said, "pressed by immeasurable suffering"; the meaning is the same.
△ Second, the explanation of the Universal Gate bestowing joy:

Possessing the power of supernormal faculties, and extensively cultivating the skillful means of wisdom, there is no land throughout the worlds of the ten directions in which he does not manifest his body.
In the prose section, the "Universal Gateway Manifestation" enumerates thirty-two bodies and traverses the lands of the ten dharma-realms;
thus, the way in which he transforms sentient beings through the three wheels of inconceivable power is exceedingly voluminous and extensive. Now, I shall summarize it in a single verse.
Yet, in meaning, there is nothing that is not comprehensive. This is an instance where what is detailed in one place is abbreviated elsewhere.

As in the section on "Extracting from Suffering," only seven hardships are listed, whereas in the "Repetitive Verses" (Gāthā), twelve are extensively expounded; yet in meaning, there is no increase. This is an instance where what is abbreviated in one place is detailed elsewhere.
△ The preceding sections on the "Reiteration of the Prose" and the "Extraction [of the Essence]" are concluded. However, following these two chapters, there are two further intentions:

the exhortation to uphold [the teaching] and the exhortation to make offerings. These are not versified here; rather, the explanation waits until the two characters "Guanyin" (Avalokiteśvara) have been fully explicated before concluding with the words:
"Therefore, one must constantly keep [him] in mind; therefore, one should prostrate. Why is this? It is because through contemplation...
Although the two characters "sound" (yīn) constitute a standalone, independent verse, its essential meaning does not go beyond the two aspects of "giving" (yǔ) and "extracting" (bá).
Therefore, it is only after the meanings of giving and extracting have been concluded that the exhortation to uphold and the exhortation to make offerings are finally presented.
△ Second, the specific explanation of Avalokiteśvara. This is not a verse following the prose; it is called a "solitary rising verse" (*guk-pi sung*).

Because one can extract from suffering simply by reciting the name "Avalokiteśvara" mentioned above, the repetition of the verses is now complete. Now, the merits of the two characters "Avalokiteśvara" are explained separately;
therefore, it is called a "separate verse. It is divided into two parts: first, explaining "Avalokita" in terms of extracting from suffering; second, [explaining it] in terms of bestowing...
Regarding the phonetics of "Lè" (Joy): in the prose section, it merely states that Avalokiteśvara removes suffering and universally bestows joy.

This would seem to imply that the name of the Great Being is partial rather than all-encompassing. Therefore, by examining this single name in detail, we see that it possesses both "bestowing" and "removing";
only then is the meaning of the Great Being’s name fully realized in its perfect universality. Furthermore, in the prose section, it only mentions that invoking the name removes suffering, but...
I wish to know what extraordinary causes and conditions exist beneath the name [Avalokiteśvara], such that a single invocation can immediately bring about deliverance.

Therefore, I shall now explain the two characters "Guān-yīn" (Contemplation-Sound): they signify perfect and wondrous contemplation; the identity of the living being and the Buddha, and the common source of resonance and response.
Therefore, he is able to extract suffering from those who share his same essence and bestow happiness upon those who share his same essence.

By using this to manifest that sentient beings who invoke Avalokiteśvara immediately evoke the fundamental Buddha of their own nature, and that Avalokiteśvara’s subsequent extraction and bestowal immediately responds to the multitude of sentient beings within their own minds, a single invocation of his name brings about the immediate fulfillment of such extraction and bestowal.
The first part is divided into three sections. First, the restatement [of the premise].

The various evil destinies from which he extracts suffering—namely, the hells, hungry ghosts, and animals, as well as the sufferings of birth, old age, sickness, and death—he causes them all to be gradually extinguished.

Now, wishing to explain in detail the Great Being’s perfect and wondrous threefold contemplation for extracting suffering, he first sets forth the various sufferings that are to be extracted. For the sake of [the Great... (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a Buddhist commentary, likely discussing the "Three Contemplations" (*san guan*) of emptiness, conventionality, and the middle way, used here to extract sentient beings from suffering.)

The noble one’s subtle contemplation takes as its object the realm of the antidote. Regarding the phrase "various [sufferings] above the three evil destinies," this extends throughout the transformation lands (nirmāṇakāya-bhūmi) outside the triple world.
Birth, aging, sickness, and death are not limited to the six realms; even up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (Samyaksambodhi), there remains subsequent birth and death.

All of these involve the shifting of causes and the changing of fruits, characterized by arising and ceasing and impermanence; however, when occurring outside the triple world, they are given a different name.

The arising and destruction [of the conditioned world] are due to conditions. This is truly because views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) bring about birth, aging, sickness, and death within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-bhava*).

The *saṃsāra* of dust-like sands, both internal and external to the realms, brings about birth, aging, sickness, and death within the transformational existence (*pariṇāmi-bhava*) caused by ignorance (*avidyā*). The subtle contemplation of the Great Being (*mahāsattva*) is fully capable of causing all these to be extinguished.

If one discusses the perfect contemplation (*pūrṇa-vipaśyanā*) of the Great Being, it should only involve the simultaneous breaking of the five abodes and the two types of death; yet, what is now spoken of as "gradual" is as follows:
It is like smelting iron: the coarse impurities fall off first.

By the very nature of things (*dharmatā*), one first extinguishes birth and death within the realm, next extinguishes birth and death both within and without the realm, and thereafter purifies and eliminates birth, aging, sickness, and death outside the realm. Immediately following this, one extracts the root that enables these [extinguishings].
△ Second, the explanation of the contemplation that can uproot [afflictions]:

The contemplation of reality, the contemplation of purity, The contemplation of vast wisdom, the contemplation of compassion, and the contemplation of loving-kindness— I constantly aspire to and constantly gaze upon them.
"True contemplation" and "pure contemplation" constitute the perfect contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā*). By means of this true emptiness, one destroys the delusions of the four abodes.
Once the contemplation of true emptiness is perfected, it universally purifies the defilements of birth, old age, sickness, and death within the six realms of ordinary beings and the evil destinies.

In antiquity, there was only the term "contemplation of emptiness"; however, because the royal house avoided the character for "emptiness," it was changed to the two characters "pure. (From the *Guang*)
The contemplation of great wisdom is precisely the contemplation of the Middle Way within the profound and immeasurable wisdom of all Buddhas.

By means of this Middle Way contemplation, one universally extinguishes the transformations of birth, old age, sickness, and death, as well as the evil destinies, arising from the ignorance of the five stages beyond the realms.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "First, within the faculty of hearing, one enters the stream and forgets the object.

This continues until one suddenly transcends both the mundane and supramundane worlds, universally extinguishing the suffering of birth and death within the two types of mundane evil realms. This achievement lies in the two contemplations of emptiness."
In short, these two [emptiness and the middle] are first required for one's own practice to destroy delusions; they are likewise appropriate as the primary means to destroy the delusions of others.

The *Jiyao* states: "To eliminate the distinction between the pure and the defiled, one employs emptiness and the middle. It further states: "As for negation, it is naturally within emptiness and the middle.
Once the evil delusions of birth and death have been destroyed, one may respond to conditions and achieve unimpeded penetration, emerging into the provisional according to circumstances.

Universally transforming sentient beings, one employs the contemplation of emptiness (假觀) to deliver them; this does not go beyond the extraction of suffering and the bestowal of happiness, which are precisely the contemplations of compassion (悲觀) and loving-kindness (慈觀).

As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Above, [the practitioner] shares the same power of compassion as the Buddhas of the ten directions. This refers to the contemplation of loving-kindness that bestows happiness.
Below, one shares the same compassion and yearning as all sentient beings in the Dharma-realm; this is the contemplation of compassion that uproots suffering.

This provisional contemplation universally extinguishes the various evil destinies, births, aging, sickness, and death of sentient beings, which is to say, it destroys the dust-like sands of evil karma.
This is because the Great Being himself employs the twenty-five kingly samādhis, wherein each and every samādhi consists of the three contemplations.

Success is achieved. Having universally extinguished the three obstacles of afflictions (*kleśa*), karma, and suffering, one then uses the merit of this fundamental method to universally shatter the three obstacles of sentient beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*.
As it is said: because the contemplation of emptiness (*śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*) is perfected, the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are shattered;

because the contemplation of the provisional (*upāya-vipaśyanā*) is perfected, the dust-like karmas are shattered; because the contemplation of the middle (*madhyama-vipaśyanā*) is perfected, the root of ignorance (*avidyā-mūla*) is shattered. Thus, the Bodhisattva themselves—
One uses the three contemplations to destroy the three obstacles; furthermore, one uses the three contemplations to universally destroy the obstacles of the twenty-five existences.
The phrase "Always vow, always gaze up" is the concluding exhortation of the Honored One.
It says that since the Great Being possesses these three kinds of wondrous contemplations which completely extinguish all sufferings, all sentient beings should, at all times...
One makes a vow, gazing up at the Great Being (Mahāsattva) to seek the cessation of suffering. Here, the character "guan" (觀) is pronounced with the departing tone (qùshēng).
Furthermore, it should be explained according to the *Biyā* (埤雅), which interprets it as "huán" (雚) meaning "to see clearly."
△ Second, the conclusion on the function of wisdom:
With stainless, pure light, the sun of wisdom destroys all darkness; it can subdue calamitous winds and fires, universally illuminating the world.

By the power of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), the various evil destinies, birth, old age, sickness, and death—the five abidings (*pañca-vihāra*) and two types of death—are entirely extinguished.

Thereupon, the dust is purified and light arises; the contemplation is perfected and wisdom is revealed. Spontaneously, the three kinds of wisdom-light are accomplished, such that their illuminating function and activity are simultaneous.
Through the perfection of the pure contemplation, the pure light arises; through the true contemplation, the defilements of the four abidings are shattered, resulting in stainlessness.
Light. Within vast wisdom, the wisdom-sun of contemplative realization (*vipaśyanā*) shatters the darkness of the five abodes and the two types of death.
As the Sūtra says: "Sitting upright, one contemplates the true nature (*dharmatā*); all transgressions are like frost and dew, which the sun of wisdom can dispel.

This refers to the practice of contemplating compassion to bestow happiness and remove suffering. Suffering belongs to the obstacle of retribution (*vipākāvaraṇa*), such as the seven calamities and other forms of karmic retribution mentioned previously. Furthermore, regarding retribution...

Regarding the three calamities of the great and small kalpas: now that the contemplation of the wondrous provisional (*prajñapti*) is perfected, one achieves the knowledge of the seeds of the path (*mārga-jñatā*).

This enables the complete uprooting of the three obstructions within the *dharmadhātu*; hence it is said that one can "subdue the winds and fires of calamity. The character "calamity" (*zāi*) is the general term, while "wind" and "fire" are the specific terms.

By citing both the general and the specific together, it is revealed how the wondrous provisional knowledge of the seeds destroys evil karma and brings to utter purity the three obstructions as numerous as motes of dust.

Thus far, we have discussed the function of perfected wisdom through contemplation and refuted all obstacles. Once the obstacles have been shattered, the three contemplations become profoundly clear, universally illuminating the Dharma-realm.

Every single world is the true realm of the *sāmbhogakāya* (the Body of Universal Radiance), and this eternal *sāmbhogakāya* land is not separate from the Sahā world, nor is it a vast void where nothing exists. This is what is meant by "not being like the triple world."

It is seen within the three realms. Because the three contemplations and three wisdoms of the perfect [contemplation] are all wondrous regarding all phenomena, it is said that "universal illumination shines upon the world.
The preceding treatise negated deluded attachments; the subsequent one clarifies the Dharma. Such is the nature of the Dharma.

Furthermore, it should be understood that previously, when the three contemplations had not yet been attained and the three obstacles had not been completely shattered, then all various things were nothing other than the evil destinies and the cycle of birth and death.
Once they have been shattered, these various elements all become the wondrous objects illuminated by Universal Radiance (Samantaprabhā).
△ Second, the explanation of sound in terms of bestowing bliss has two parts. First, it first demonstrates that the two wheels are the basis of sound.
The thunderous roar of the precepts, whose essence is compassion; the wondrous great cloud of a benevolent mind: it pours down the nectar-rain of the Dharma, extinguishing the flames of affliction.
Desiring to proclaim the three kinds of sounds and to bestow happiness by expounding the wondrous Dharma in its three cycles, [the Buddha] first brings forth the foundation of his teaching.

Because the body and mind have long been perfected through compassion (*karuṇā*), one is then able to rain down the Dharma from the wheel of speech to extinguish the flames. "Body" here refers to compassion;

it is precisely this great compassion that causes one to enter the burning house. Furthermore, this wheel of the body must necessarily arise from the *vijñapti* (informative) and *avijñapti* (non-informative) precepts.
It is accomplished through maintaining the precepts purely without transgression. Regarding the phrase "the thunderous roar of the precepts":

when the practitioner completes the four *karmas*, the light of the precepts from the ten directions enters the crown of the practitioner’s head with a sound like the collapse of a mountain or an earthquake. This can be seen by those with the divine eye or who possess saintly power;

therefore, it is metaphorically likened to a thunderous roar. As for the intention behind naming it "Compassion" (*maitrī*): it is as the scripture says, "By what kind of body should one be delivered? Third.

The seven practices, such as contemplating trees and walking meditation, mostly involve discerning the capacities [of sentient beings] with the desire to bestow the Dharma-joy of the four supramundane teachings;
is this not compassion? Furthermore, regarding the "great cloud":

just as a cloud can contain rain, and as worldly people say, "Everyone looks toward this cloud for rain," so too does the mind contain the rain of the Dharma. Words are the manifestation of the mind; that is, one speaks from within the mind.

The Dharma-gates contained therein are like the pouring down of nectar-rain. When the Wheel of Sound preaches the Dharma, it sustains the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom of sentient beings, just as the immortal nectar of the devas does.

One should know that these teachings spoken by the Wheel of Sound are all achieved through the long-term perfection of the body’s discipline of great compassion and the long-term accumulation of the cloud of the mind’s great kindness; only then can they employ the Wheel of Sound to propagate the transformation of beings.

△ Second, the actual emergence of the three sounds, all of which bestow bliss. Regarding the "three sounds": these refer to the sound of the Dharma, the sound of metaphors, and the sound of causes and conditions that surpasses the mundane.
This is divided into two parts. First, the sound of mindfulness bestows bliss.
"In the midst of litigation before the authorities, or amidst the terrors of a military array, by recollecting the power of that Avalokiteśvara, all enemies shall retreat and disperse.

The mention of "litigation" and "military arrays" seems to continue the previous twelve difficulties without exhausting them; by recollecting the power of Avalokiteśvara, all are able to retreat and disperse.

This text is identical to the section on "extracting from suffering," yet it is now categorized as "bestowing happiness. Hereafter, the characters for the name [Avalokiteśvara] are correctly explained.
The emphasis lies on the aspect of bliss. That is to say, within the Universal Gate (*samantamukha*), it concerns the sound with which he manifests whatever body is appropriate to preach the Dharma.

Since this teaching of the Dharma is definitively established as being for the purpose of bestowing bliss, it is provisionally so named. However, if one discusses its true essence, bestowing [bliss] and extracting [suffering] occur simultaneously;
yet, one cannot use a general principle to challenge a specific instance. Since it is said that [beings] are terrified and retreat, how could they not experience joy?
△ Second, the actual emergence of the three sounds:
"Wondrous Sound, Avalokiteśvara; Brahma-sound, ocean-tide sound; surpassing all worldly sounds.
These five characters of sound all specifically designate the Great Being as the voice that preaches the Dharma. As for the Dharma preached:
This definitely refers to the wondrous Dharma. One must not, because of the phrase "observing its sounds," erroneously judge it to be the voices of sentient beings.
If one treats it as the sound of karmic resonance, both the text and the meaning are lost. Wondrous sound is precisely the sound of the Middle Way’s contemplation of the true reality;

it can propagate the wondrous Dharma, yet those with the capacity for the Middle Way are not numerous. When a Great Being emerges from the provisional to deliver sentient beings, he must furthermore...
He surveys the world at large to discern the capacities and conditions of beings, distinguishing between their ailments and the medicines required as numerous as dust motes or grains of sand.

Having fully understood all this, he then teaches and transforms them with the sound of the Dharma; this is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) that issues forth provisional sounds. "Brahma" means purity.
When the wisdom-observation of true emptiness stands before one, the ultimate truth is directly revealed; thus, the defilements of afflictions are purified entirely without remainder.
As it is said, "The ultimate truth is the sublation of all phenomena.

This is the Great Being’s propagation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-exposition—the wondrous Dharma that circulates throughout the Middle Kingdom—by means of the Dharma-sound of the perfect and subtle Three Truths and Three Contemplations, universally transforming all sentient beings.
It causes them to attain the joy of opening, showing, awakening, and entering. The "ocean-tide voice" is a metaphor: the tides within the ocean are extremely reliable and predictable;
they never deviate from their timing, whether advancing or retreating. When the Great Being preaches the Dharma, he perfectly accords with the capacities and needs of sentient beings;
he never errs by speaking either too early or too late. For if he were to speak before the capacity has been stirred, or fail to speak once the opportunity has passed, [the teaching would be lost].

For example, when the tide is expected at the hour of Zi on the first and fifteenth days of the lunar month, yet it instead occurs during the hours of Si and Wei, one’s trust is betrayed and the timing is missed.
Now, the Dharma-voice of the Great Being is like a great bell suspended upon its frame: it rings as soon as it is struck. It is like a bright mirror set upon its stand:
whatever form appears before it is immediately reflected. Neither preceding nor following, it accords precisely with the capacity of those to be guided, just like the ocean tide.
The Great Being uses this analogy of sound to propagate the Tathāgata’s analogical teaching of the wondrous Dharma that pervades all.

Regarding the phrase "surpassing the sounds of the world," the Tathāgata further feared that sentient beings would not understand how the Great Being’s preaching of the Dharma accords with their capacities;
therefore, he set aside the metaphors of the Dharma and directly pointed it out, saying: "In total, this is the Great Being’s response."
The sound of their seeking is superior to the speech and sounds of you worldly people. Among worldly people, those who violate their promises are few in their trustworthiness.
When others seek assistance in times of urgency, they may grant verbal consent while harboring no intention to give;
or when others seek rescue in times of distress, they may feign compliance with their mouths yet fail to dispel the hardship or resolve the conflict. Even if there are pleasant words...
As for speech, although he offers prayers and music, he ultimately does not participate in them; this is the sound of worldly people. The Great Being is not like this.
When people encounter suffering and distress and call out for help, he immediately rescues them upon their request.
When people practice cultivation even slightly and seek happiness, he grants that happiness everywhere; it is as described in the long prose section above. This is not merely the making of a vow.

At that time, everyone granted their permission for [the gift] to be taken away; yet when it came to seeking actual assistance, they were entirely devoid of substance—people in this world who speak empty words.

By means of this sublime Dharma-sound concerning worldly causes and conditions, the Mahāsattva extensively propagated the wondrous Dharma of causes and conditions as taught by the Prince in worlds as numerous as the dust motes of the past, following the Tathāgata’s own exposition. Indeed, since this chapter...
This pertains to the uniquely wondrous person and dharma of the dissemination; it cannot be explained through casual or scattered interpretations.

This is truly because the Great Being came from the East, preaching the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, and was endowed with these three kinds of wondrous voices. Thus, he was able to propagate the wondrous Dharma of the Threefold Cycle of the Honored One.
Moreover, these sounds were precisely suited to the sentient beings of this Sahā world whose faculty of hearing is most acute.
Therefore, it is fitting that you should propagate the sublime Dharma within this Sahā world to deliver all living beings; this is not something that other bodhisattvas can hope to equal.

△ Third, the triple conclusion and exhortation regarding upholding and making offerings, in two parts: first, the conclusion and exhortation to uphold the name; second, the conclusion and exhortation to perform prostrations and make offerings. (Prose section)
