Having extracted [beings] from the seven calamities and other sufferings, he immediately concludes by exhorting them to uphold the Name. Having universally bestowed happiness through the Universal Gate, he immediately concludes by exhorting them to pay homage and make offerings.
Now, he simply waits until the independent section on Avalokiteśvara is complete before finally bringing forth the two preceding conclusions;

therefore, they are called "repeated conclusions. This is truly because the separate exposition of Avalokiteśvara is sufficient to cover only the two aspects of bestowing [happiness] and extracting [suffering] through compassion. It is not...
Setting aside other matters for the moment, we shall therefore wait until the conclusion is reached before summarizing; thus, there will be no interruption in the meaning. Now, for the first part:

For this reason, one must maintain constant mindfulness, never allowing doubt to arise in every thought-moment regarding the Pure and Holy Avalokiteśvara, who [rescues] from the perils of suffering and death.
It can act as a refuge;

because it can serve as a refuge from the perils of suffering and death, one must constantly keep it in mind. This concludes the exhortation to uphold [the practice] for the purpose of uprooting suffering.
△ Second, the conclusion and exhortation to offer worship:
Possessing all merits, beholding sentient beings with eyes of compassion, an ocean of merit immeasurable—therefore, one should prostrate with the crown of the head.

Beholding sentient beings with eyes of compassion is the bestowing of happiness; a mass of merit like the ocean is able to bestow happiness. Therefore, one should pay homage. This is an exhortation to offer worship and prostration;

it is a verse that reiterates the aforementioned exhortation to offer worship by bestowing happiness. Question: The long prose version speaks of "making offerings" (*pūjā*), whereas here it says "paying homage" (*vandana*).
How are these two reconciled? Answer: "Making offerings" encompasses the four types of requisites; it includes the presentation of pearls, prostration, and respectful salutation.

Regarding these dharmas: what was previously called "making offerings" (pūjā) refers to the general [category], whereas what is now called "prostrating" (praṇipāta) refers to a specific instance within that offering.
Although the general and the specific are presented alternately, their meaning is one and the same. Question: The prose section provides exhortations; why is there now a summary?

Answer: Whether one encourages [the practice] by assigning it to specific groups or encourages it collectively, there is no contradiction in meaning. However, by slightly shifting the sequence, the flavor of the text becomes even more profound and enduring.
Furthermore, because one perceives that the teaching of the Dharma is harmonious and integrated, and that the eloquence is unimpeded, one does not fall into the criticism of being dull or pedantic.

Question: In the prose section, two chapters are presented separately; the former provides a comparative evaluation, while the latter clarifies the offering of gifts. Why are these matters treated with such gravity and detail?
[Question]: "All [of them]. Why now do you speak of only a few phrases? [Answer]: "When the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma, he values only the manifestation of its meaning, not the quantity.
As it is said: 'Whether many, they possess the four virtues; whether few, they also possess the four virtues. Whether extensive, they are Prajñā; whether abbreviated, they are also Prajñā.'"
A single bright pearl—how could it not possess all manner of treasures? To further explore the Buddha’s intent, the emphasis lies in revealing the Great Being and extolling compassion.
As for the exhortation to make offerings and uphold the Name, the meaning seems somewhat secondary and may be concluded briefly.

Moreover, since the preceding section has already been extensive and detailed, this portion should be summarized with key points; through the mutual illumination of the extensive and the concise, the purport of the exhortation becomes even more evident. It need not be [further elaborated].
One must entertain doubt.
△ Second Major Section: Conclusion on Benefits.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Sthavira Dharaṇīdhara rose from his seat, approached the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, if there are sentient beings..."
"Those who hear this chapter on the Sovereign Acts of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the Universal Gateway’s Manifestation of Supernatural Powers should know that their merit will not be small.
When the Buddha had spoken this Chapter on the Universal Gateway,
eighty-four thousand beings within the assembly all resolved to attain unexcelled, perfect, and complete enlightenment, which is peerless.
The *Dharanidhara-parivarta* provides a further layer of praise for the Honored One that seems even deeper than the preceding sections.
Indeed, when the Great Master himself extols his deluded disciple, his compassion and grace reach their ultimate limit. Who would dare offer words of praise beyond this?
Yet, Dharanidhara suddenly rose from his seat and addressed the Buddha: "What wisdom could possibly surpass that of my teacher, such that it might supplement what is lacking in my teacher?"
This is clearly revealed [in the scriptures]. Kṣitigarbha stated that it is only after sentient beings invoke the name of Avalokiteśvara that their suffering is extracted;
only after mental recollection is the poison extinguished; only after prostration is the request fulfilled; and only after making offerings does he manifest his form to bestow bliss, and so forth.
If those in the world who cannot recite his name, pay homage, or make offerings were not saved by the Great Beings,
would this not mean that the Great Beings lack the compassion of universal connection? One must know that even if they do not recite his name, pay homage, or make offerings,
if they merely hear this Sūtra on the Bodhisattva’s Universal Gate and Supernatural Powers spoken today, you should know that the merit of such a person is no small matter.
Merely hearing this sutra brings no small merit; how much more so for upholding its name with mindful recitation?

How much more so for prostrating and paying respectful homage? And how much more so for making offerings to the full extent of one's ability? May I ask what kind of benefits are obtained—surely they are not few.
If [the merit] were merely to escape the three miserable realms and be born in the three happy paths, then the merit would be small. But if...

If one distances oneself from the six realms of ordinary beings, the merit realized by attaining the fruits of the Two Vehicles is still slight; if one abandons the Lesser Vehicle to enter the Bodhisattva path, the merit is likewise slight.
Ultimately, what great benefit is gained from hearing this sutra? Only then can it be said that it is not slight.
As for those present at this current Dharma assembly, when they hear the Buddha preach this "Universal Gateway" chapter, there are eighty-four thousand among the multitude.
All who are born [in this state] give rise to the peerless *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* mind, continuing until they attain Buddhahood;
indeed, they are not few. Those who merely hear the *Pumen jing* (Universal Gate Sutra) and gain understanding through its names and characters give rise to the mind of the Unsurpassed Way;

how much more so for those who practice the five grades of devotion—recitation, mindfulness, prostration, and offering—who, through their semblance and ultimate stages, attain the Unsurpassed Right [Enlightenment].
"How awakening! This Chidi [Dhṛtarāṣṭra] has heard this sutra so superficially; how much more so would it be for one who practices profound prostrations!
At first, he seemed to dismiss what the Buddha praised, saying: "Much is not necessarily attained; much is not necessarily attained.

It is sufficient merely to hear the name of this sutra; its merit reaches the unsurpassed. This reveals a vision that far surpasses his own teachers. Subsequently, he took the shallow benefit of hearing the sutra as a further advantage.

The manifestation of form and the upholding of ritual involve profound merit; furthermore, there is the merit of relying upon a teacher. How could this be compared to mere superficial or redundant words?
This concludes the superficial exposition on the "Universal Gate" chapter of the Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva Sūtra.
